source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone
finding: Core claim: objectives are deceptive in hard problems. Rewarding only behavioural difference from past behaviours (a novelty score: mean distance to the k nearest neighbours in the current population plus an archive of past novel behaviours) can solve tasks that direct goal-seeking fails on. Novelty search is not random search: it keeps an archive and still explores systematically.
numbers: Novelty = average distance to k nearest neighbours in behaviour space. An individual enters the permanent archive if its novelty exceeds a threshold. Same NEAT settings for all arms; only the reward scheme differs.
limits: Needs a hand-built behaviour characterisation fitted to the domain. The authors say the novelty measure must be fitted to the domain.
agent_relevance: Open mode: a scored difference-from-what-was-already-tried signal can escape a deceptive goal gradient. The agent needs a task-specific description of what counts as a different attempt.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone - medium maze
finding: On the medium deceptive maze both novelty and fitness NEAT solved it in every run, but novelty was about 3x faster. Random selection solved it in only 21 of 40 runs, so novelty is not random.
numbers: Novelty: 18,274 evaluations (sd 20,447). Fitness: 56,334 (sd 48,705). 40 runs each, p<0.001 (Student t). Random selection: 21/40 runs. Solution size: fitness 66.74 connections (sd 56.7) vs novelty 24.6 (sd 4.59), p<0.05.
limits: One simulated robot maze, 2 maps. Solved = end within 5 units of goal. 250,000 evaluation cap.
agent_relevance: Novelty search also gave simpler solutions here. Suggests a lean-solution side effect, not yet shown for language agents.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone - hard maze
finding: On the hard, highly deceptive maze, fitness-based search almost never succeeded and was no better than random selection, while novelty search almost always succeeded.
numbers: Novelty: 39/40 runs solved, 35,109 evaluations on average when solved (sd 30,236), 33.46 connections. Fitness NEAT: 3/40. Random selection: 4/40.
limits: Same single domain. Success judged under a 250,000-evaluation cap.
agent_relevance: When the objective signal is deceptive, following it is no better than chance; a different-from-before signal is needed. Supports doubting only on a stall signal (G1).

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone - unenclosed maze (boundary condition)
finding: Failed case: when the behaviour space is unbounded (two walls removed), novelty search lost its advantage because it is easy to be novel by wandering outside the maze.
numbers: Novelty solved 5/100 runs; fitness solved 2/100. Not significantly different.
limits: Novelty needs a behaviour space where being new correlates with useful progress. Fitness also failed, so the authors note fitness was no real alternative.
agent_relevance: Open mode needs a bounded, meaningful novelty axis. Free-form be-different on text can drift into irrelevant variation.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone - bounded archive
finding: The archive can be capped as a queue the size of the population without hurting performance in this maze.
numbers: Archive limited to 250 (population size): 40/40 solved, 38,324 evaluations (sd 42,229), not significantly different from the unbounded archive.
limits: Maze only. Authors note some backtracking is possible.
agent_relevance: A short memory of past attempts may be enough; no need to keep everything in context.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone - coarse behaviour grids (conflation)
finding: Coarsening the behaviour description barely hurt novelty search, except at the smallest grids. But using fitness itself as the behaviour description (conflating distant states) hurt a lot.
numbers: Grids larger than 4x4: largely unaffected; only 4 of 960 runs failed within 500,000 evaluations. 4x4 grid (16 behaviours): 117,107 evaluations on average, about 3x slower. Fitness-as-behaviour: 11/40 solved vs fitness NEAT 4/40 (p<0.05, one-tailed Fisher).
limits: Maze only. Authors frame the rule as respect the stepping stones, not simply less detail is worse.
agent_relevance: Warning for any novelty judged on a single score: merging different paths into one number hides stepping stones.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone - biped locomotion
finding: In a 3D biped walking task, pure novelty search evolved controllers that walked farther than fitness-based search, again with smaller networks.
numbers: 50 runs: novelty 4.04 m (sd 2.57) in 15 s vs fitness 2.88 m (sd 1.04), p<0.01. Connections: fitness 272.90 (sd 178.97) vs novelty 87.52 (sd 48.22), p<0.001.
limits: Mean advantage is modest and novelty has larger spread. One simulator.
agent_relevance: Gains transfer beyond mazes but are smaller and noisier than the maze headline.

source: Lehman & Stanley (2011) Abandoning Objectives: Evolution through the Search for Novelty Alone - deception argument and prior remedies
finding: The paper defines deception as a fault of the objective function: the gradient leads away from the goal. It reviews remedies that still depend on the objective (diversity maintenance, niching, multi-objectivization) and argues they do not remove deception.
numbers: No pooled numbers for the remedies.
limits: Argument section, not an experiment.
agent_relevance: Diversity-by-niche inside an objective-ranked pool is weaker than a pool ranked by novelty; our pool design should keep the two signals separate.

source: Gomes, Mariano & Christensen (2015) Devising effective novelty search algorithms: a comprehensive empirical study
finding: Independent systematic re-test of novelty search on six mazes (30 runs each, 180 per treatment). Tuning matters: k near 15 works; a random archive beats a novelty-based archive; pure novelty is beaten by blending with fitness.
numbers: Success ratio best for LS-50 (50/50 novelty and fitness blend) and NSGA (multi-objective), not different from each other (p=0.75), both better than all others (p<0.01). Random archive best; k in [15,100] best for novelty archive (p<0.05). No archive with k=199 (whole population) was significantly worse than all other evolutionary treatments.
limits: Maze domain only; authors say the optimal novelty weight may be task dependent. A 75% novelty weight (LS-75) gave little benefit over pure novelty and was worse than LS-50 (p<0.01).
agent_relevance: Pure novelty is rarely the best policy. Blend with the objective, as G1 and the schema imply. Hybrid beats either alone.

source: Gomes et al. (2015) - PMCNS hybrid and behaviour-space size
finding: A previously successful hybrid (progressive minimal criteria novelty search) was generally ineffective here. It beat pure novelty only on low-deception mazes and lost on highly deceptive ones. Mazes differ in how much reachable behaviour space is irrelevant: Open 99.5%, Subset 85%, Zigzag 60%, Hard 30%.
numbers: PMCNS: no significant advantage over pure novelty except share of high-fitness individuals (p<0.01). Better on star and zigzag, worse on hard and multi mazes.
limits: Partial failed replication of earlier positive PMCNS reports (refs 8, 10, 11 in the paper). Higher mutation rates did not improve behaviour-space exploration.
agent_relevance: Positive reports from one lab can fail on another set of mazes. Treat any single novelty trick as conditional on the deception level.

source: Gomes et al. (2015) - exploration uniformity
finding: Measured how evenly novelty search covers behaviour space apart from solving the task. NSGA kept uniformity just below pure novelty while reaching solutions faster. Novelty search benefited from lower mutation rates than fitness search.
numbers: NSGA had higher uniformity than LS-50 (p<0.001). Each treatment 180 runs (6 mazes x 30).
limits: Mazes only; uniformity is defined on that maze behaviour grid.
agent_relevance: Report a coverage measure in open mode alongside success, so the pool is checked for spread.

source: Mouret & Clune (2015) Illuminating search spaces by mapping elites
finding: MAP-Elites: keep the best solution found in each cell of a user-chosen feature grid, pick a random filled cell, mutate it, and place the child in its cell if it beats the incumbent. It is the simplest quality-diversity (QD) algorithm and the base of most LLM-era open-endedness work.
numbers: Three domains (modular neural nets, simulated and real soft robots). Soft robots: MAP-Elites better than controls on reliability and coverage (p<0.002). Single best solution: no significant difference from the two optimisation controls (p>0.05).
limits: The arXiv version is a preliminary draft; the author note says data are subject to change. MAP-Elites was significantly worse on precision than the optimisation controls (p<0.01) because evaluations spread over many cells.
agent_relevance: A grid of niches with one elite each is a cheap way to hold diverse partial solutions. Matches a state design with an archive of candidate hypotheses by type.

source: Pugh, Soros & Stanley (2016) Quality diversity: a new frontier for evolutionary computation
finding: Defines QD as search for many high-quality solutions that differ, and the QD score (sum of best quality per niche). Listed here only because ELM and QDAIF (both opened) use its metric.
numbers: QD score = sum of champion performance across niches, as used in ELM and QDAIF.
limits: Not opened by me this session.
agent_relevance: QD score is a usable single-number check of diverse and good for a candidate pool.

source: Conti et al. (2018) Improving exploration in evolution strategies for deep RL via a population of novelty-seeking agents (NS-ES, NSR-ES, NSRA-ES)
finding: Brings novelty search to deep RL: NS-ES (novelty only), NSR-ES (average of reward and novelty), NSRA-ES (adaptive weight). On a humanoid with a deceptive trap, plain ES got stuck every run; the novelty variants escaped and the hybrids did best.
numbers: Humanoid with trap, 10 runs: ES stuck in the trap in every run; NSR-ES better than NS-ES and ES (p<0.01); NSRA-ES better than NS-ES and NSR-ES (p<0.01). Meta-population M=5 (Atari M=3, k=10).
limits: Small run counts (5 per Atari game). Novelty alone often gave lower reward. NS-ES and NSR-ES were worse than ES on Alien, Gravitar and on humanoid without the trap, so novelty costs when exploration is not needed.
agent_relevance: Strong support: raise exploration only after a stall (adaptive weight rises when stuck) instead of always. Same logic as G1.

source: Conti et al. (2018) - Seaquest case and Atari
finding: On Atari Seaquest, plain ES flatlines at a local optimum (never surfacing for air). Novelty variants surface and score higher. NSRA-ES fell into the same trap at first because it began on reward and shifted weight slowly.
numbers: Seaquest median reward: ES 960; NS-ES 1044.5 (p<0.05); NSR-ES 2329.7 (p<0.01), 5 runs. 12 Atari games tested; behaviour description = concatenated RAM states.
limits: Novelty biased toward longer trajectories (distance not normalised). I could not read the multi-game table reliably from the PDF text, so it is not quoted.
agent_relevance: Timing of the switch matters: switching too slowly kept the stall. A stall detector should trigger fast.

source: Ecoffet et al. (2021) First return, then explore (Go-Explore, Nature)
finding: Go-Explore keeps an archive of reached states, returns to a promising one, then explores from it. It fixes forgetting of good states (detachment) and exploring before returning (derailment). It beat the state of the art on hard-exploration Atari.
numbers: Montezuma's Revenge: robustified mean 1,731,645, 150x the previous state of the art and above the human record (about 1.2 million). Pitfall: mean 102,571 (max 112,000) while earlier algorithms scored 0 under sticky actions. Exploration phase exceeded human score on all 55 Atari games. Private Eye: max score in 4 of 5 runs.
limits: Needs a simulator that can restore states (or a goal-conditioned policy). Domain-knowledge cell representation helps a lot. A separate robustification step is required.
agent_relevance: Template for an archive-plus-return loop: keep a library of reachable partial states, resume from them, then branch. Close to checkpointed states.

source: Wang, Lehman, Clune & Stanley (2019) Paired Open-Ended Trailblazer (POET)
finding: POET co-evolves environments and agents. New environments are accepted only if neither too easy nor too hard (minimal criterion), and agents are transferred between environments as stepping stones. It solved environments that direct optimisation and a direct-path curriculum could not.
numbers: 2-D bipedal walker; success threshold 230. ES alone on two POET-made environments: best scores 24.0 and 19.2, far below 230. Each run used 256 CPU cores; ES population 512; 5 ES runs per comparison.
limits: Handcrafted environment encoding (gaps, stumps, roughness) bounds novelty. The direct-path control could sometimes solve the lowest difficulty targets.
agent_relevance: A not-too-easy, not-too-hard filter plus transfer between problems is the open-mode pattern for choosing next problems. Needs an LLM-readable difficulty signal.

source: Wang et al. (2020) Enhanced POET: open-ended reinforcement learning through unbounded invention of learning challenges
finding: Adds a general environment encoding (CPPN), a domain-general novelty measure (PATA-EC: rank agents' performance across environments), better transfer, and the ANNECS progress metric (accumulated number of novel environments created and solved). Direct ES, PPO and a manual ground-interpolation curriculum fail on mid and late POET targets.
numbers: Controls significantly underperform POET on middle and late stage targets (p<0.01, Wilcoxon signed-rank). Original POET ANNECS plateaued after about 20,000 iterations; Enhanced POET kept rising nearly linearly (5 runs, 95% bootstrap CI), slowing slightly after 30,000.
limits: Authors ask whether even Enhanced POET is petering out. 5 runs only. 2-D walker only.
agent_relevance: Open-endedness stalls when the generator vocabulary is fixed; the generator must keep widening. A problem generator for an LLM agent needs a rich space.

source: Tao, Francois-Lavet & Pineau (2020) Novelty Search in Representational Space for Sample Efficient Exploration (NeurIPS)
finding: The Tao et al. 2020 key work. Novelty reward is the k-NN distance in a learned low-dimensional latent space, shaped by an information bottleneck and a relative-distance loss so pixel noise does not count as novel; combined with planning in latent space (depth 5).
numbers: Steps to reach the goal (lower is better; 5 trials, Welch t-test): Acrobot novelty 576.0 (SE 66.13) vs baselines 592.5 to 1713.3; multi-step maze novelty 524.6 (SE 73.24) vs baselines 658.8 to 1863.3.
limits: Not significant against the best baseline in each task (Acrobot p=0.85, maze p=0.23 for the closest). Deterministic environments only; stochastic-density baselines dropped. k-NN cost grows linearly with steps. Only 5 trials.
agent_relevance: Novelty must be measured in a learned meaningful space, not raw surface form. For text agents: compare attempts by approach and meaning, not wording.

source: Lehman et al. (2020) The surprising creativity of digital evolution: a collection of anecdotes
finding: Collects reports from many researchers where evolving systems found unexpected, often unintended solutions, including exploits of simulation bugs. Open search surprises its designers, and stated objectives get satisfied in letter and not in spirit.
numbers: Anecdote collection from dozens of contributors; no aggregate statistics.
limits: Anecdotal and selected; not a controlled study.
agent_relevance: Warns that optimising a stated goal can exploit loopholes; supports checking on held-out items (G3).

source: Lehman et al. (2022) Evolution through Large Models (ELM)
finding: An LLM-trained diff model is the mutation operator inside MAP-Elites. Starting from one hand-written, barely functional Sodarace walker, it filled almost all niches and made hundreds of thousands of working designs in a domain absent from training data. This data then trained an LLM that outputs valid walkers conditioned on terrain.
numbers: Grid 12x12x12 = 1,728 niches (height, width, mass); fill averaged over three runs per seed; nearly all seeds fill the map. Fine-tuning the diff model on accepted diffs raised niches reached, QD score and share of valid diffs. A 300M diff model was used in the bug-fix test.
limits: Seed choice mattered: the Radial seed scored high QD but exploited chaotic dynamics and gave poor downstream RL, so was excluded. The conditional model often collapsed to one unconditional solution.
agent_relevance: LLM mutation beats random mutation because it makes coherent multi-part edits. An LLM can be the variation operator while code does selection and bookkeeping (G5).

source: Bradley et al. (2023) Quality-Diversity through AI Feedback (QDAIF)
finding: An LLM judges both quality and diversity of generated text, so MAP-Elites can run on creative writing (opinions, stories, poetry) without hand-coded features. Compared with fixed-prompt, shuffled few-shot, random-search and quality-only baselines.
numbers: QDAIF had higher QD score than baselines in all domains (5 seeds, bootstrapped 95% CI; max QD 20, or 100 for the 2D archive). Human study: QDAIF human QD score competitive with or better than baselines in Opinions and Stories; per-cell human scores about 0.6 to 0.87.
limits: Small human sample. An LLM judge of diversity is subjective. Fixed-prompt baselines were less reliable.
agent_relevance: Supports using an LLM as novelty and quality judge in open mode, but judge noise and verbosity bias (G5) must be handled; do the scoring in code over fixed categories.

source: Zhang, Lehman, Stanley & Clune (2024) OMNI: open-endedness via models of human notions of interestingness (ICLR)
finding: Learnable is not enough; tasks must also be interesting. A foundation model (GPT-4, few-shot) filters tasks by interestingness on top of learning progress. OMNI beats uniform sampling and learning progress alone in Crafter and BabyAI.
numbers: Crafter: 15 interesting tasks diluted with 90 boring repeats (e.g. collect N wood) and 1,023 extremely hard distractors; PPO for 100M steps. Higher average task success and more tasks above 0.2 success than uniform or learning-progress-only (exact values are in figures, not in text I read).
limits: Exact numbers only in figures. Boring tasks are synthetic numeric repeats, which suits an LLM filter. Learning progress is still computed statistically, not by the model.
agent_relevance: The filter worth doing is the missing half of novelty. A cheap LLM filter on proposed sub-problems may prevent drift into trivial variants.

source: Faldor et al. (2025) OMNI-EPIC: open-endedness via models of human notions of interestingness with environments programmed in code (ICLR)
finding: Foundation models write the task and the simulated environment code, check success with a model-written function, keep an archive, and use a model of interestingness. Controls without the archive or without interestingness did worse.
numbers: 5 runs per method; ANNECS-OMNI significantly higher than controls (p<0.05, Mann-Whitney U) and still rising at the end. Diversity measured as cell coverage in a 2D PCA of text-embedding-3-small embeddings.
limits: Authors cannot rule out that environments mirror training data. The long run used simulated learning; the short run used real RL training. Interest judged by a model.
agent_relevance: Archive plus interestingness filter are both needed. Retrieving similar past tasks as context keeps the generator from repeating itself.

source: Wang et al. (2023) Voyager: an open-ended embodied agent with large language models
finding: An LLM agent in Minecraft with an automatic curriculum that maximises novel discoveries, a skill library of verified code, and iterative prompting. It explored far more than ReAct, Reflexion and AutoGPT.
numbers: 63 unique items in 160 prompting iterations, 3.3x as many as baselines; 2.3x longer distance. Diamond pickaxe: Voyager 19 +/- 3 iterations (3/3 trials) vs ReAct, Reflexion, AutoGPT 0/3 within 50 iterations. Ablations: random curriculum cut discovered items by 93%; removing self-verification cut them by 73%.
limits: Baselines re-implemented by the authors; three trials for zero-shot tests; uses GPT-4.
agent_relevance: Curriculum from current state plus a verification gate gives most of the value. Self-verification being the biggest single factor fits G2 and G3: check from real outputs.

source: Hughes, Dennis et al. (2024) Open-endedness is essential for artificial superhuman intelligence (ICML)
finding: Position paper. A system is open-ended, for an observer, if it keeps producing artifacts that are both novel (not predictable by the observer's model) and learnable (the observer's prediction improves with more history). Argues foundation models plus open-ended search is the route to superhuman systems and flags safety issues.
numbers: Formal definition through observer, novelty and learnability. No new experiments.
limits: Position paper, no measured result. The definition depends on a chosen observer.
agent_relevance: A testable criterion for open mode: novel to the observer's model and learnable by it. Usable as a stop rule when output is neither.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) Darwin Godel Machine: open-ended evolution of self-improving agents (ICLR)
finding: A coding agent edits its own code. An archive of all agents is kept and parents are sampled in proportion to performance and inversely to number of children. It beat a no-self-improvement baseline and a no-open-ended-archive baseline (only the latest agent kept).
numbers: SWE-bench Verified 20.0% to 50.0%; Polyglot 14.2% to 30.7%. Without the archive, one bad self-edit makes later progress harder.
limits: Baseline numbers are only in figures. The paper has a section on hallucinated tool use and reward hacking. Cost is high.
agent_relevance: Strong recent LLM-agent evidence that keeping weaker but different stepping stones beats greedy hill-climbing, provided gains are checked on an external benchmark.

source: Samvelyan et al. (2024) Rainbow Teaming: open-ended generation of diverse adversarial prompts
finding: MAP-Elites over risk category x attack style, with an LLM mutator, a pairwise LLM preference judge, and a BLEU filter against the parent. Found many successful attacks on safety-tuned models; fine-tuning on the archive closed most of the gap.
numbers: After 2,000 iterations: attack success about 92% on Llama 2-chat 7B and Llama 3-Instruct 8B, 98% on Mistral 7B and Vicuna 7B (GPT-4 judge, 100-prompt archives, 3 runs). Fine-tuning Llama 2-chat 7B on the archives cut success from 92%/95% to 0.3%/0.7% on 300 held-out prompts. Transferred prompts kept about 50% of original success. Agreement on 100 pairs: human-human 83%, human-GPT-4 81%, human-Llama Guard 78%.
limits: Judges are LLMs with 78 to 83% human agreement. Targets are mostly small open models; GPT-4o results were lower (0.48 on one metric).
agent_relevance: A fixed grid of descriptors plus pairwise judging is a practical way to force diversity in an LLM sampler, and it is code-controlled (G5 compatible).

source: Stanley & Lehman (2015) Why greatness cannot be planned: the myth of the objective [book]
finding: Popular statement of the stepping-stone argument: ambitious goals are reached through paths that do not look like the goal. Recorded only for the claim's origin.
numbers: No numbers.
limits: Not opened. The evidence base is the 2011 papers above.
agent_relevance: Source of the open-mode philosophy; keep it as motivation, not evidence.
